title: The Digital Pharmacy Gap in Kenya
body:
Medicine is increasingly becoming part of the digital economy.

Customers can search for products online, communicate with pharmacies remotely, make digital payments and have medicines delivered. Kenya already has much of the digital infrastructure required for this transition: the Communications Authority's Q4 FY2024/25 statistics recorded approximately **43.75 million smartphones** and **47.7 million mobile-money subscriptions** by June 2025.

But medicine is fundamentally different from most products sold online. A conventional e-commerce transaction can often be reduced to:

**Product → Cart → Payment → Delivery**

Pharmaceutical commerce requires considerably more control around that transaction.

A medicine may be prescription-only. It may belong to a particular batch with a specific expiry date. It may need to be stored under particular conditions. It may require professional review before dispensing. A transaction may also need to remain traceable if a product is recalled or a dispensing decision needs to be investigated. This makes digital pharmacy not simply an e-commerce problem, but a **healthcare, regulatory and systems-engineering problem**.
